title: Newcomer Settlement Supports
summary: Check status → Triage → Connect → Sequence → Review
subtitle: Turn the first-year list into a route map instead of a competitive paperwork event

blocks.text: Canada’s first-week checklist can look as if someone emptied a whole filing cabinet onto a welcome mat. The trick is not doing it all today. It is knowing which step opens the next one.

Settlement groups help newcomers who qualify with housing, language classes, jobs, school, health care, meeting people and daily life. Many services paid for by IRCC are free. Who qualifies for federal help depends on your immigration status and, for some economic-class permanent residents, how long ago you got that status. Provinces, territories, cities and local groups may offer more help under their own rules.

Use IRCC’s service finder to look up funded helpers by postal code and type of help. A helper can check what you need and point you to the right place, so you do not have to search every program alone.

items.title: “Newcomer help is only available from paid immigration consultants.”
items.text: Settlement groups give free, practical help to people who qualify. Immigration legal advice is a different service. If you need someone to act for you legally, check that they are allowed to.

blocks.text: IRCC: Find free newcomer services
Knowing which free help you qualify for saves you from paying for things a settlement worker does at no cost.
blocks.detail: Your status and your permanent-resident date decide which door opens, and for how long it stays open.
blocks.extra: Section 02 shows which door is yours.

sections.title: Your Immigration Status Decides the Federal Door

blocks.text: The same welcome mat leads to different federal doors, depending on your immigration status.

items.title: USUALLY QUALIFY
items.text: Permanent residents, protected persons, resettled refugees, people IRCC has told they were picked to become permanent residents, and some temporary residents on special programs.

items.title: USUALLY OUTSIDE THE FEDERAL RULES
items.text: Most temporary residents, refugee claimants and Canadian citizens fall outside the regular federal settlement rules. Local or provincial services may still help.

blocks.text: Since April 1, 2026, economic-class permanent residents and the family who came with them usually have six years from their permanent-resident date to use federally funded settlement help. That window drops to five years on April 1, 2027.
Pre-arrival help is free for people who are approved to move here but still live outside Canada. It can help you plan, look for work and find contacts before your suitcase meets Canadian winter.

items.title: “Every newcomer has the same service eligibility for the same length of time.”
items.text: Your status, immigration class, permanent-resident date, citizenship, where you live and some special programs can all change which help you get.

blocks.text: IRCC: Settlement-service eligibility

sections.title: Get Settled, Get Connected, Then Build

blocks.text: The checklist is not a race. It is an order of steps.

items.title: Get safe and settled
items.text: Housing, food, urgent health care and a way to reach people come first. A settlement worker can help with each one.

items.title: Get your key papers
items.text: Apply for your SIN and provincial health card, open a bank account and sign the children up for school or childcare.

items.title: Start language and job help
items.text: Book a language test, join a free class, and ask about job search and how to get your training recognized.

items.title: File taxes and claim benefits
items.text: File a tax return every year, even with little or no income, so benefits like the Canada Child Benefit can reach you.

blocks.text: LINC and CLIC are free English and French classes for adult newcomers who qualify. You usually take a language test first. Class times, child-minding, travel help and online options depend on the provider.

How your foreign training is recognized depends on your job and your province. Find the group that licenses your job before you pay for a review or a course. A handsome receipt is not a professional licence.

items.title: “A foreign degree must always be replaced with a Canadian degree.”
items.text: Some jobs are regulated and need a review or a licence. Others are not. Your best route may be a review, a bridging program, a certificate, proof of your past work or a direct job search, not always a whole new degree.

blocks.text: Key takeaway: check what help you qualify for first. Then take each step in the order that opens the next one: safety, papers, language, work and benefits. Use free official and community help before you pay, and update your plan when your status, province or family changes.

sections.title: Farah Builds a Route, Not a Pile

blocks.text: Meet Farah
paragraphs: Farah Haddad lands in Winnipeg as a permanent resident with an engineering degree, two children and a checklist long enough to count as hand luggage. Her goal is clear. She wants to work as an engineer again before her savings run out.

In week two, an ad finds her. A private company offers a “Canadian certification package” for $2,400. It promises a faster path to engineering work. Farah has not yet found out who licenses engineers in Manitoba.
Meanwhile, the list keeps growing. The kids need a school. She needs a health card. She cannot go to a single class or interview without someone to watch the children.
The deadline on the ad is Friday. Paying feels like progress, and she has the money. Farah opens the payment page, then closes it. She decides to spend one free hour with a settlement worker first.

The worker helps her check her service window, book a language test and find childcare for her classes. Then they look up Manitoba’s engineering regulator together. It wants an assessment through its own process. The $2,400 package is not part of it.

Three months later, Farah has a real plan to get licensed, a short list of jobs to apply for and fewer appointments. The package ad still turns up now and then. She keeps it in a folder called “not today.” The paperwork is still paperwork, but it has stopped forming its own government.

blocks.text: In Quebec, settlement help works under a separate federal-provincial deal. Use Quebec’s official newcomer services as well as federal immigration information.
What resolved the conflict?
A paid package is not the same as finding your regulator. Check your service window and the real requirements before you spend money on either.
Farah kept $2,400 and found her real path to licensing by talking to a free settlement worker before she paid.
blocks.detail: One free hour with the right helper can show you what to do first and what can wait.
blocks.extra: The quick check in Section 05 tests whether you can spot the next step.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Why check your immigration status before choosing a settlement service?
items.detail: Federal help depends on your status. For some economic-class permanent residents, the date you got that status also sets a time limit.

items.title: What changed in 2026 for many economic-class permanent residents?
items.detail: Since April 1, 2026, they usually have six years from their permanent-resident date to use federally funded settlement help. That drops to five years on April 1, 2027.

items.title: What usually happens before a LINC or CLIC class?
items.detail: You usually take a language test first. Class times, child-minding, travel help and online options depend on the provider.

items.title: Why find your job’s regulator before paying for a credential service?
items.detail: How your training is recognized depends on your job and province. A receipt from the wrong group does not give you a professional licence.

items.title: Why file a tax return even when your income is low?
items.detail: You may need a filed return to get benefits that depend on income, even when you earned little or nothing.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): First-Year Settlement Route Map

blocks.text: Write short notes only. Keep your passport, UCI, SIN, health card, bank and immigration numbers in safe official places, not in this form.
A settlement plan is a set of steps, not a race. Never share passwords or one-time security codes, and ask whether a copy of a document is needed before you hand one over.

items.title: Settlement provider
items.text: A group that helps newcomers settle into life in Canada.

items.title: Permanent resident
items.text: A person with permanent resident status who is not yet a Canadian citizen.

items.title: Protected person
items.text: A person given protection under Canadian immigration law.

items.title: Pre-arrival service
items.text: Settlement help you can use before you move to Canada.

items.title: LINC/CLIC
items.text: Free English or French classes for adult newcomers who qualify.

items.title: Regulated occupation
items.text: A job that needs approval from a provincial or territorial body.

items.title: Credential recognition
items.text: Checking school, training or work done in another country.

quiz.question: True or False: “Newcomer help is only available from paid immigration consultants.”

questions: What is your immigration status, and when did you get it? An approximate date is fine.
What is your most urgent need right now? For example, housing, food, health care or childcare.
Which settlement helper will you contact first? Write “not sure” if you have not found one yet.
Which papers do you still need? For example, a SIN, a health card or a bank account.
Do you plan to take a free language class? (Yes / No / Not sure)
What is one job or training step you will take in the next 30 days?
samples: Childcare, so I can go to classes.
The newcomer centre near my home. I found it with IRCC’s service finder.
A provincial health card for my youngest child.
Yes. I booked my language test for next week.
Look up my job’s regulator in Manitoba before I pay for anything.
